desc: Section 1687 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024 is the moment the SAP architecture and the UAP question meet in enacted law. Subsection (a): 'None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act may be obligated or expended in support of any activities involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations unless the Secretary of Defense has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.' Subsection (b) closes the industry-funded route: consistent with DoD Instruction 3204.01, 'independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership'. The definitions widen the audience well past 10 U.S.C. 119(g): 'appropriate congressional committees' means the congressional defense committees plus both intelligence committees, and 'congressional leadership' means the majority and minority leaders of the Senate and the Speaker and minority leader of the House. Three things follow. First, Congress enacted, on 22 December 2023, a funding prohibition premised on the possibility that UAP activity was being run under special access or restricted access limitations without being reported - a premise it would not have legislated against had it been satisfied no such activity existed. Second, subsection (b) targets precisely the mechanism by which a contractor can fund work internally and recover it as overhead, which is the route that does not appear in any appropriation line. Third, by naming the AARO fiscal year 2024 report, Congress tied the prohibition to a specific document rather than leaving it abstract.

Sec. 1687(b) provides that 'independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by' DoD Instruction 3204.01, and carries the codification note '50 USC 3373 note'.

Sec. 1687(c)(1) defines 'appropriate congressional committees' as the congressional defense committees plus the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence and the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence; (c)(2) defines 'congressional leadership'.
Subsection (a) is limited to funds made available by that Act and so lapses with the fiscal year, while subsection (b) carries no fiscal-year limitation and is codified as a note to 50 U.S.C. 3373.

Section 7343 of the FY2024 Intelligence Authorization Act imposes the same limitations on intelligence funds, running through the Director of National Intelligence rather than the Secretary of Defense.

dossier.narrative:
Section 1687 does not repeal or amend 10 U.S.C. 119(e). It leaves the waiver lawful and operates on the money instead: the waiver may still be exercised, but funds authorised by this Act cannot be spent on a UAP-related special access activity that Congress has not been told about. That is a materially different instrument from an oversight reform, and it is the instrument Congress reached for.

The two subsections have different reach and it matters. Subsection (a) is limited to 'funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act', so it expires with the fiscal year. Subsection (b), the IR&D allowability bar, carries no fiscal year limitation at all and sits as a note to 50 U.S.C. 3373. One was a one-year appropriations rider; the other was meant to persist.

Neither the FY2025 NDAA (P.L. 118-159) nor the FY2026 NDAA (P.L. 119-60) re-enacted the 1687(a) prohibition, which is recorded on this board as a full-text search finding rather than an inference.
openQuestions: Whether any programme was actually reported to the appropriate congressional committees under 1687(a), and whether any funding was withheld as a result.
Whether subsection (b)'s IR&D allowability bar has ever been applied to a specific contract, and by which contracting officer.
Why neither the FY2025 nor the FY2026 NDAA re-enacted subsection (a), and whether anything replaced it.
dossier.whatItIs: Section 1687 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, Pub. L. 118-31, 137 Stat. 621, titled 'Limitation on Use of Funds for Certain Unreported Programs'. It has three subsections. (a) bars obligation or expenditure of funds authorised by the Act on any UAP-related activity 'protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitation' that has not been reported to Congress. (b), carrying the codification note '50 USC 3373 note', makes UAP-related independent research and development unallowable as an indirect expense under contracts covered by DoD Instruction 3204.01. (c) defines 'appropriate congressional committees' as the congressional defense committees plus HPSCI and SSCI, and imports the 50 U.S.C. 3373(n) definition of 'unidentified anomalous phenomena'.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the point where the SAP architecture and the UAP question meet in enacted law rather than in testimony. Congress does not write a targeted funding prohibition, or a targeted bar on a specific category of contractor overhead recovery, for a subject matter it believes is absent from the portfolio. The provision is the legislature acting on the possibility that UAP work was being carried inside special access programmes it had not been told about, and inside contractor IR&D it was indirectly paying for. Its companion, section 7343 of the FY2024 Intelligence Authorization Act, imposes the same limits on intelligence funds through the DNI rather than the Secretary of Defense, so the pair covers both sides of the DoD/IC seam.

entityInfo.desc: The full operative text of Sec. 1687, Public Law 118-31, enacted 22 December 2023. Subsection (a): 'None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act may be obligated or expended in support of any activities involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations unless the Secretary of Defense has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.' Subsection (b): 'Consistent with Department of Defense Instruction Number 3204.01 (dated August 20, 2014, incorporating change 2, dated July 9, 2020; relating to Department policy for oversight of independent research and development), independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership.' Subsection (c) defines the appropriate committees as the congressional defense committees plus both intelligence committees, and congressional leadership as the four party leaders. Section 7343 imposes the identical structure on intelligence appropriations through the Director of National Intelligence. Neither provision has produced any publicly reported disclosure.
